claims.evidence: NHS About page: you will usually only take metoclopramide for a short time.
claims.newSentence: The NHS says metoclopramide is usually taken for a short time. [cite About page, not side-effects page]

claims.evidence: MedlinePlus tablet page: treats GERD (heartburn/reflux) and gastroparesis (slowed stomach emptying).

StatPearls excerpt: antagonises central and peripheral D2 receptors in the medullary chemoreceptor trigger zone (area postrema). 'Mainly used as an anti-sickness medicine' not in returned StatPearls text.
claims.newSentence: StatPearls describes metoclopramide as blocking dopamine-2 receptors, including in the chemoreceptor trigger zone of the brainstem.

claims.evidence: A review excerpt says 'in the basal ganglia, metoclopramide inhibits dopamine receptors causing dopaminergic-cholinergic imbalance', but the search blended pages and the specific URL was not confirmed as NBK519517; the lay gloss of the basal ganglia is general knowledge.
claims.newSentence: Keep text; drop or re-verify the NBK519517 citation.

claims.evidence: Review excerpt links akathisia, acute dystonia, drug-induced parkinsonism and tardive dyskinesia to this mechanism; source page not confirmed for NBK519517; plain-English glosses are general knowledge.
claims.newSentence: Keep text; drop or re-verify the NBK519517 citation.

claims.evidence: NHS: most common side effects are feeling sleepy and diarrhoea; low mood or depression is in the common list.
claims.newSentence: Drowsiness, low mood or depression, and diarrhoea are listed by the NHS as common side effects.

claims.evidence: NHS side-effects page covers feeling dizzy (stop what you are doing, sit or lie down).
NHS: the most common serious side effect is uncontrollable movements such as tics, tremors, muscle stiffness and spasms.
Tablet page: TD may persist after stopping. 'Risk rises with longer treatment' came from the injection page, not the tablet page.
claims.newSentence: MedlinePlus, a US source, says tardive dyskinesia, a movement disorder, may not go away after metoclopramide is stopped. Its injection page adds that the risk rises the longer treatment lasts.

claims.evidence: MedlinePlus tablet page: older adults (65 and over) usually should not take it for GERD/gastroparesis as other medicines are safer; US source already labelled.
NHS: call 999 or go to A&E if you have a seizure or fit; wording clearly on how-and-when page, side-effects page reported to match but blended.
claims.newSentence: The NHS says to call 999 or go to A&E straight away after a seizure or fit while taking metoclopramide. [cite How and when page plus side-effects page]

claims.evidence: NHS: avoid alcohol; it will make you feel more sleepy (About page). A second NHS page is softer ('best not to drink').
claims.newSentence: The NHS advises avoiding alcohol with metoclopramide because it will make a person feel more sleepy. [cite About page]

claims.evidence: StatPearls excerpt: patients who develop NMS should stop metoclopramide; 'rare, life-threatening' not in returned text. The 999 advice comes from NHS (call 999 if you think you might be having NMS), not StatPearls.
claims.newSentence: StatPearls describes neuroleptic malignant syndrome as a possible complication of metoclopramide. The NHS says to call 999 if you think you might be having it. [cite StatPearls plus NHS How and when page]

notes: Seizure 999/A&E confirmed on NHS how-and-when page (side-effects page reportedly matches). NHS alcohol: About page says avoid, will make you sleepy; another NHS page is softer. NHS pages ~2 years old per search. StatPearls URL returned as ?report=reader/printable variant. mechanism[2]/[3] retained as textbook; citation unconfirmed.
